intro: Le Gibet, marked Très lent, is the second piece of Ravel’s Gaspard de la nuit. It is a setting of Aloysius Bertrand’s poem of a gallows at sunset, and a repeated B♭ sounds like a bell throughout while chords move around it.

sections.label: A · Repeated B♭ octave, Très lent
sections.mNote: A repeated octave sounds above slow chords.

sections.label: B · Chords above and below the bell
sections.mNote: The hands pass the B♭ between them.

sections.label: C · Bare melody, without expression
sections.mNote: The bell moves below the exposed upper line.

sections.label: Dev · Fuller chords over the B♭
sections.mNote: Fuller chords return around the unchanged B♭.

sections.label: Coda · Bell B♭ over low held notes
sections.mNote: Low held notes and the B♭ remain at the close.

cues.title: Repeated B♭ octaves
cues.text: A B♭ in octaves repeats throughout while slow chords move beneath it, in a rhythm independent of theirs. Ravel marked the piece Très lent and asked for the soft pedal throughout.
cues.evidence: Durand score (1909), plate D. & F. 7207, p. 17: Très lent, Sourdine durant toute la pièce, repeated B♭ octaves. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6a/IMSLP246875-PMLP02576-Ravel,_Maurice-Gaspard_de_la_nuit_Durand_7207_scan.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bertrand’s poem Le Gibet
cues.text: Bertrand’s poem lists small, horrible sounds near a hanged man, among them a fly at the dead man’s ear and a spider making his necktie. The source is named in the line “C’est la cloche qui tinte” — “It is the bell that tolls.” Beyond the town walls, the setting sun reddens the hanging body.
cues.evidence: Aloysius Bertrand, Le Gibet, Gaspard de la nuit, Mercure de France edition (1895), pp. 245–246; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Le_Gibet

cues.title: Ravel and Aloysius Bertrand, 1908
cues.text: Ravel and Ricardo Viñes read Aloysius Bertrand as students, along with Baudelaire, Poe and Mallarmé. A new edition in 1908 brought Ravel back to him. He wrote Gaspard, “three romantic poems of transcendental virtuosity”, between May and 5 September, and Viñes gave the first performance on 9 January 1909.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner’s programme note (https://geraldlarner.com/work/ravel-gaspard-de-la-nuit-1908) gives the student reading with Viñes, the 1908 Mercure de France edition (which he says “must have” revived Ravel’s interest), the composition between May and September 1908 and Ravel’s own phrase. Manuel Cornejo’s chronology (https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf) dates the composition to 5 September 1908 and the première, by Viñes at the Société nationale, to 9 January 1909.

cues.title: Repeated B♭ on three staves
cues.text: Ravel writes the piano part on three staves. High and low chords move around the repeated B♭, which passes between the hands. Where the chords fill the keyboard, the B♭ continues to sound inside them.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 18: three-stave writing, alternating m.d. and m.g. indications for the bell, with chordal lines above and below.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Upper melody over the B♭
cues.text: A melody enters in the upper register above the repeated B♭. Ravel marks it un peu en dehors, mais sans expression, slightly brought out but without expression. The B♭ continues below it unchanged.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, first system: pp un peu en dehors, mais sans expression over the repeated low B♭.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the tied chords
cues.text: The piano texture fills out again in long, tied chords. The bell note, still B♭, sounds between them. Ravel’s instruction from the first page still applies: “without hurrying or slowing to the end”.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, lower systems. Ravel’s instruction Sans presser ni ralentir jusqu’à la fin appears on p. 17; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording, Kaisersaal, 2020
cues.text: OE1FEU made this recording of the piece on a Bechstein D 282 concert grand in the Kaisersaal, and dated it 3 April 2020. It was released under a Creative Commons Attribution–ShareAlike licence.
cues.evidence: Commons file description (own work, Bechstein Konzertflügel D 282, Wiener Kaisersaal, date 2020-04-03, licence CC BY-SA 4.0): https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maurice_Ravel-_Gaspard_de_la_Nuit-_II_Le_Gibet.flac

cues.title: Final page, repeated B♭
cues.text: On the last page the melodic fragments stop. Low bass notes are held under the repeated B♭, and the final bars drop to ppp. The B♭ continues until the last chord.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 20: low held bass, repeated B♭ and final ppp chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Three staves around the B♭
transitions.from: A · Repeated B♭ octave, Très lent
transitions.to: B · Chords above and below the bell
transitions.how: The piano writing expands to three staves, with low held notes, the recurring B♭ and chords high above it. The two hands share the bell, and the upper chords are marked très lié, very smoothly joined. The B♭ is repeated through each change of harmony.
transitions.evidence: Durand score (1909), pp. 18–19: three-stave writing and the continuing B♭.

transitions.title: Upper melody above the low bell
transitions.from: B · Chords above and below the bell
transitions.how: The fuller chords thin out. A single upper line, marked pp and sans expression, crosses above the B♭ in the bass. Each of its long notes is held across several strokes of the bell.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, first two systems: exposed melody and low repeated B♭.

transitions.title: Tied chords and the six-flat signature
transitions.to: Dev · Fuller chords over the B♭
transitions.how: The single upper line broadens into tied chords as the six-flat key signature returns. The B♭ bell continues between the hands, above a sustained low bass. Small crescendo hairpins mark the chords, and the slow tempo does not change.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 19, third and fourth systems: six-flat signature, tied chords and crescendo hairpins.

transitions.title: Return to the opening bell texture
transitions.from: Dev · Fuller chords over the B♭
transitions.to: Coda · Bell B♭ over low held notes
transitions.how: The high chords diminish, and the piano goes back to the slow bell-and-chord writing of the opening. Deep sustained notes lie under B♭ octaves. The repeated figure gets softer, moving through p, pp and ppp. Ravel’s instruction to keep the same pace applies through to the end.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 20; the instruction to keep the pace appears on p. 17.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
